query: For a titanium- and nickel-containing high-entropy alloy in a single-phase solid-solution state, whose elevated-temperature mechanical performance remains unestablished when titanium and nickel serve as primary constituents rather than additions, what single testable intervention hypothesis could produce better mechanical properties under elevated-temperature or extreme-environment testing than the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, mechanism, predicted relative outcome, applicable composition and test-regime boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Applying severe plastic deformation (via high-pressure torsion) followed by a brief low‐temperature aging treatment to a single‐phase Ti–Ni-based high‐entropy alloy will induce nanoscale domains of chemical short‐range order (SRO) and refine the dislocation structure. This SRO will enhance beneficial cross‐slip and impede unstable dislocation motion, yielding significantly improved elevated‐temperature tensile strength and enhanced creep resistance compared to the same alloy processed without this deformation/aging intervention.
generation.material_initial_state: A single‐phase, FCC-structured high-entropy alloy primarily composed of titanium and nickel (with additional stabilization elements to maintain a single solid solution) produced, for example, via directed energy deposition without SPD or post-aging treatment.
generation.intervention: Subject the as-deposited alloy to severe plastic deformation via high‐pressure torsion (e.g., ~6 GPa, 5 rotations) at room temperature, followed by a controlled low‑temperature aging treatment (e.g., 600 °C for 1 hour).
generation.conditions: Elevated-temperature mechanical testing—tensile and creep tests—performed in the range of approximately 750 °C to 1000 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: The creation of a high density of dislocations and nanoscale regions exhibiting chemical short‑range order (SRO) without forming secondary brittle intermetallic phases; concomitant grain and subgrain refinement enabling enhanced dislocation cross-slip and increased resistance to dislocation climb at high temperatures.
generation.mechanism: The severe plastic deformation introduces high dislocation density and local composition fluctuations that act as nucleation sites for SRO during the subsequent low-temperature aging. The resulting nanoscale SRO domains increase the local barriers to dislocation motion—particularly reducing the rate of unfavorable double-kink nucleation in screw dislocations—while enhancing cross-slip in edge dislocations. Together with the refined microstructure, these effects improve yield strength and retard creep deformation under high temperature conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to an identical alloy without SPD/aging, the treated alloy is predicted to show a higher elevated-temperature tensile yield strength and longer creep rupture life due to enhanced cross-slip-induced strengthening and microstructural stability under extreme conditions.
generation.baseline: The same Ti–Ni-based high-entropy alloy produced by DED or a similar process and tested in its as-deposited condition without severe plastic deformation or aging treatment.
generation.boundary: This intervention is applicable to single-phase Ti–Ni-based HEAs designed to be thermally stable up to about 1000 °C, and its benefits are expected for tensile and long-term creep tests in that temperature range. The study is limited to alloys where the formation of deleterious intermetallics can be avoided by proper control of processing and composition.
generation.uncertainty: While prior studies (e.g., PMC8357793::web::003) document the influence of chemical SRO on dislocation mobility in refractory HEAs and other work (e.g., PMC11123020::web::001 and PMC5627260::web::006) highlights the role of Ti in solid solution strengthening, it remains uncertain whether the controlled induction of SRO via SPD plus aging in a primary Ti–Ni system will generate the desired nanoscale ordering without triggering unwanted phase separation. The exact balance between beneficial SRO formation and the risk of brittle intermetallic precipitation requires careful experimental optimization.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples of the same Ti–Ni-based high-entropy alloy using identical deposition parameters. Apply high-pressure torsion (HPT) followed by low-temperature aging to one set while leaving the other set in the as-deposited state. Characterize the microstructure (via TEM, SEM, and atom probe tomography) for evidence of SRO and grain/subgrain refinement. Then conduct high-temperature tensile and creep tests (750–1000 °C) on both sets.
measurements: Microstructural characterization to detect nanoscale chemical SRO and quantify dislocation density and grain size.
Elevated-temperature tensile yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and elongation measurements.
Creep rupture life under specified stress and temperature conditions.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the SPD/aging-treated alloy does not show statistically significant improvements in elevated-temperature yield strength and creep rupture life compared to the as-deposited baseline, or if the microstructural analysis reveals either no SRO formation or the emergence of deleterious secondary phases, then the hypothesis that the intervention improves mechanical properties via induced SRO is falsified.
